_README: Enrichment bookkeeping removed from rendered route prose: sentences addressed to whoever maintains the database, printed to climbers as beta. Thirteen ended their descent text with an instruction to a column ("Set rappels to 0."). The climbing fact beside each one is kept; only the instruction goes. Findings that existed ONLY in these notes were moved to research-data/DEFECT-TRIAGE-2026-08-19-CLUSTERED.md first, so the sweep loses nothing.

set.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — descend by reversing the North Ridge exactly as ascended; there is no rappelling on the standard route. From the summit, downclimb the steep snow/small-tree section back to the top of the 5,400 ft cliff band, then carefully reverse the rising traverse and gully bypass on the east side of the crest to regain the ridge crest below the cliffs — this bypass is the one spot demanding real route-finding and careful downclimbing (loose rock and exposure in the gully), so many parties down-face here rather than walk it. Below 5,200 ft, follow the open rocky ridge back into the brushy, exposed 4,500-5,200 ft stretch, staying on the crest to avoid the steep drop-offs to either side. Once back into old-growth forest below 4,500 ft the ridge broadens and travel gets easy and fast; one trip report notes the descent takes well under half the time of the ascent once past the brush and cliff band. Continue down through the second-growth/deadfall lower forest to regain FR 68 at the East Fork Foss River bridge pullout near mile 5.2. No technical anchors (bolted or natural) are used on this route — it is entirely natural terrain.

This is a scramble with no rappelling — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the black-hornfels summit, downclimb the northeast ridge (Class 2-3, loose in spots) back down to the east-face scree/talus, which is noticeably looser and more hazardous descending than ascending — plan on a slow, controlled downclimb with attention to kicking rock onto anyone below. Continue down the scree/talus to the col, then reverse the off-trail traverse (talus edge, then NNE across the grassy/rocky basin) back over to Shellrock Pass, re-bypassing the snowfield if it was present on the way in, and drop back to camp in Shellrock Basin. From there the return to the trailhead simply reverses the multi-day trail approach: Shellrock Basin to Shellrock Pass, over Rolo Pass, past Fred's Lake, down to and along the Middle Fork Pasayten River, back up over Slate Pass, and out to the Robinson Creek/Buckskin Ridge Trailhead. No technical gear (rope, rack, harness) is needed anywhere on this route; a helmet and trekking poles/ice axe (for any lingering snow near Shellrock Pass) are the only extras worth carrying. This is a full walk-off/downclimb.

set.approach: This crag's coordinates correspond to the Hannegan Pass/Ruth Creek Valley area near Mt. Baker, sometimes referenced as 'Ellation Crags,' a minor, lightly-developed granite cragging/multipitch area. The general access is from I-5 Exit 255, east on SR-542 (Mt. Baker Highway) about 46 miles, then a left onto Forest Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road) for about 4 miles to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Beyond that trailhead, published approach details for the crag itself are sparse and inconsistent, so the exact on-foot route and distance are not confirmed.

set.descent_text: Cosley-Houston is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. From the summit area, follow the boot track (or break a new one) toward Colfax's secondary/eastern summit, then contour around its south side just below the top — no technical downclimbing is required on a normal-conditions descent. This drops you to the Colfax-Baker col (the Baker-Colfax saddle). From the saddle, pick up the standard Coleman-Deming route down the Coleman Glacier, roping up again and watching for the same crevasses navigated on the way up (some trip reports note trending to the glacier's right side to find solid bridges late-season). Continue down to the moraine, then the Heliotrope Ridge Trail back to the trailhead. Give yourself a real daylight margin for this: multiple trip reports specifically warn against descending the glacier after dark, and parties that summit late have ended up down-climbing the icy trail by headlamp. There is no rappelling on the standard descent.

Nearly all parties reverse the ascent line (Southeast Glacier / upper Northeast Ridge route) rather than finding a separate walk-off: downclimb the Class 3 ridge (one short, more exposed Class 3+/4 move is commonly reported near the summit ridge, and some parties carry a short hand line for one airy notch — this is a fixed handline, not a rappel) back to the north-side notch, downclimb (or belay, if icy) the steep snowfield/gully back onto the Southeast Glacier remnant, cross the glacier roped and mindful of crevasses, descend the loose Class 3 gully back into the upper basin, then retrace the boot path and Copper Creek Trail to Holden Village. Multiple trip reports for this route explicitly describe downclimbing the ascent line — one notes glissading available snow where possible — and none report rappelling; this is a downclimb/walk-off route, not a rappel descent.

set.rappel_count_note: Two rappels, and this count assumes two 60 m ropes doubled through natural horn anchors — that is the published kit for the route and a single rope does not link the stations. Both anchors are slung granite horns rather than fixed hardware, so carry replacement webbing. Per-station distances are not published; the listed values are estimates from the description of the first rappel as roughly a 120 ft double-rope rappel and should not be planned around.

set.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling. Retrace the ascent line: descend the same Class 2 talus/scree slope back down to Fortune Creek Pass, taking care on the loose scree (many parties find it faster and safer to plunge-step or glissade lingering snow in the gully in early season rather than fighting the talus). From the pass, drop back onto the maintained Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394 and follow it back down through the meadows and forest to the trailhead, retracing the ~3.5 mi hike-in. The two summits of Esmeralda Peaks are close enough that some parties traverse between the east and west high points along the connecting ridge before descending the same southwest gully — this adds minor Class 2-3 ridge scrambling but no additional technical gear. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are reported on this route; the only real descent hazards are loose rock underfoot and reduced visibility route-finding back to the correct gully in whiteout/low-cloud conditions given the broad, similar-looking talus slopes above Fortune Creek Pass.

No rappelling — this is a full glacier/snow walk-off, reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the Disappointment Peak Cleaver ridge back to the 9,600 ft col, then descend the Cool Glacier to the 9,100 ft col. Cross back beneath Disappointment Peak on the return traverse staying climbers' left (i.e., lower, farther from the peak) this time to reduce time exposed under active rockfall — trip reports specifically note ascending right/descending left as the safe pattern here. Crevasses on the Cool Glacier open up significantly by mid-to-late season, with reports of 'house-eating' cracks near the col and snow bridges that weaken through the summer — rope up and probe suspect bridges, and expect the safe line to shift as the season progresses. Continue down to White Pass and out the North Fork Sauk River Trail to the trailhead.

This is a walk-off/glacier descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the pumice Sitkum ridge back to the ~9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, then descend the Sitkum Glacier's upper section, staying in the corridor left of the icefall/rock rib that splits the glacier's lower half, back down to Boulder Basin. Crevasses exist on the Sitkum but are sparse and generally avoidable with standard route-finding; a rope, harness, and a few pickets are still standard kit. From Boulder Basin, follow the steep climbers' path back down to the PCT/White Chuck Trail junction and retrace the White Chuck River Trail to the trailhead.

Reverse the ascent line — the correct SE-ridge descent is generally easier to pick out looking downhill than it was on the way up, and most parties who wandered onto the harder Class 4 rock on the ascent spot the easier Class 3 bypass ('sidewalk' ledge) on the way down. From the true summit, downclimb the short (~100 vertical foot) summit block via its broken south-side terrain rather than traversing climber's-left, which dead-ends above the exposed south face in sustained 4th-class ground. Continue down the scree/talus climber's-left of the SE ridge crest back to the Foggy Lake outlet on the same cairned line used on the ascent, then retrace the maintained Gothic Basin trail — through the basin meadows, the steep timbered switchback band, and the Weeden Creek ford — back to the Barlow Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling required in normal summer conditions. The real hazards are loose rock and fall exposure on the summit block and upper scree, and, in early-season or wet/icy conditions, hard snow on the slabs and snowfield just below the ridge, where an ice axe (and caution on the creek crossing) is warranted. A short handline is occasionally carried by conservative parties for the final summit-block downclimb, but it is not standard gear for this route.

This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly used on this route. Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the steep step back through the summit notch, reverse the granite-block and talus traverse back to about 4,800 ft, then follow Klinger Ridge's meadow/boulder terrain back down. Because the true east ridge crest was found to cliff out / not reasonably traverse in recent trip reports, most parties drop off the ridge into the small basin/tarn area below Klinger Ridge rather than trying to hold the crest, then pick up the ascent streambed line back to the 4,300 ft rock basin. From there, reverse the talus-and-streambed line down through the heathered slope and huckleberry brush to road's end at 3,480 ft, favoring the mossy streambed over bashing straight through brush (watch footing on wet moss). No technical rope work has been reported on this route; a short handline could be a reasonable option for less-confident parties at the summit notch step, but it is a downclimb, not a rappel. Primary hazards on the way down are the same as the approach in reverse — brush, slick streambed rock, and route-finding in fog on a trail-less, partly fire-scarred mountainside — plus the general scramble hazard of downclimbing loose granite steps.

There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb, reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the slabs back to the col/notch between Hagan's twin summits, re-cross the moat, and retrace the rising traverse around the Hagan Glacier's ice apron (rope up again if you did on the way in — moat and crevasse hazard is the same in both directions). Continue down the broad scree/talus couloir to the heather benches on the south flank, then descend back through the two cliffbands — this is the trickiest part to reverse cleanly since the weaknesses threaded on the way up are easy to lose from above; take note of your ascent line (photos, cairns, or a GPS track) before committing. From below the cliffbands, continue the steep bushwhack descent past the small tarn ('Hidden Lake') back down to the Baker River valley floor, rejoin Baker River Trail #606 near Sulphide Creek Camp, and hike the remaining ~2.6 miles out to the trailhead. Parties who combine Hagan with Mount Blum or a longer Blum-Hagan-Bacon traverse typically continue over connecting ridges/cols instead of reversing this line, but for a standalone South Slopes ascent, downclimbing the ascent route is the standard descent. Because of the loose rock in the couloir and the brushy, unmarked cliffband sections, the descent is commonly reported as slower and more error-prone than the climb — budget extra daylight.

set.beta: One of Jack Mountain's roughly seven established lines, nearly all class 4. A class-4 'Southeast route' and a 'South Face' are recorded separately, distinct from a harder, direct 5.6/Grade III 'Southeast Ridge' first climbed in 1977.

Goatshead Spire is documented only by its location (Lemah Two's east spur), approximate elevation, and first-ascent party/date; no grade, pitch count, or detailed route description has been published.
set.descent_text: No descent description for the spire exists. Plan on rappelling what you climb, which on an unrepeated 1982 line means carrying enough cord and slings to build and leave anchors. Below the tower, the retreat is the reverse of the approach: back down through the cirque, down the snow finger, down the class 2-3 step beside the small waterfall, then the flagged climbers' path on the north bank of Lemah Creek back to the PCT, and 7-plus trail miles out via the PCT junction and Pete Lake. Budget for finishing in the dark — parties on the neighbouring standard route routinely do.

The standard descent is a walk-off, not a rappel-the-face descent. From the notch below the true summit (not the summit itself), head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left — roughly 20 feet of 3rd-class terrain. Old rap slings are present in this gully but most parties simply downclimb rather than bother rigging a rappel. From the base of the gully, traverse right (north) until you intersect the well-worn climbers'/cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to join the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road-walking versus following Blue Lake Trail all the way to its own trailhead. Some parties instead choose to rappel directly back down the East Face route itself (useful in bad weather or if the walk-off is unfamiliar/snow-covered) — one documented descent of the face took 7 double-rope (60m) rappels, built from a mix of slung horns/rap rings and a couple of fixed/bolted anchors encountered on route. That face-rappel line is not the recommended standard descent, just an alternative to the normal walk-off descent.

set.beta: A January 2002 ascent recorded as 'Lichtenberg Mountain West Face 5.9+' was made by James Nakagami, climbing with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall — the implicit pitch for the crag. A 'grand west face' is separately listed as one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and a party is on record as having been turned around by the sheer wall before eventually reaching the summit by an easier line, which corroborates that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: back down through the exposed summit notch onto the west ridge/west face slopes, then down to the Chief Creek drainage and the Waptus River Trail for the long walk out. The notch just below the summit is the one real technical spot. Many parties simply downclimb it (class 3-4, exposed but with positive holds); others choose to protect it with a single short rappel — roughly 30-50 ft — off a sling/cordelette around a chockstone or horn. No bolted or fixed anchors are reported anywhere on this peak (the rock throughout the Little Big Chief massif is consistently loose/choss), so plan to build and retrieve a natural anchor; a single 30m rope is more than enough for this one rappel. This matches the pattern on the mountain's other aspects — parties on the north ridge and on the Falcon/Northwest Face route both report a single short rappel or two off natural anchors right at the summit block — so a short, single-rappel (or downclimb-only) exit is the reasonable expectation here too. Below the notch, retrace the talus/heather slopes back to the Chief Creek ford, re-cross the Waptus River below the lake, and reverse the Waptus River Trail back to Salmon La Sac; this is a long enough approach/descent that most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a base camp near Chief Creek or Lake Ivanhoe rather than a car-to-car push.

Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the west ridge/upper scramble terrain back through the false-summit area to the top of the lateral moraine above Green Creek cirque, staying alert for loose olivine blocks that are easier to kick loose on the way down. Cross back over the moraine and pick up the flagged Green Creek climber's path to rejoin Elbow Lake Trail #697 near the Hildebrand Creek switchback, then follow the maintained trail back down through old growth to the Middle Fork Nooksack crossing and out to the FSR 38 trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no fixed rappel stations reported on the standard line. That said, parties on adjacent Twin Sisters summits occasionally encounter short steep gully sections where a single-rope rappel or handline is used for extra security on wet or snow-covered rock; if conditions or a party's comfort level warrant it, a short single-rope rappel (30m single-strand off a natural anchor — block, horn, or sling around a boulder, since there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this peak) could substitute for a downclimb on the steepest step, but this is optional and not part of the standard descent. The biggest descent hazards are the loose moraine crossing and losing the unmarked climber's path in whiteout/dusk conditions — note landmarks on the way up, and the Middle Fork Nooksack ford should be re-evaluated for rising afternoon glacial melt before crossing back.

This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route. Reverse the scramble exactly: downclimb the ledgy, loose upper 1,000-1,100 ft back along the red-arrow line past the Sandalee Glacier snowfield/talus shelf and around the lower sub-summit to the top of the main talus field below Heaton Camp. Multiple trip reports specifically flag the descent as the more dangerous half of the trip — loose, gravelly ('kitty litter') slab sections sit right above significant exposure, so downclimb deliberately, stay right on the marked route, and consider a helmet for the scramble portion. Once back on maintained trail at Heaton Camp, it's a long reversal of the approach: roughly 6-7 miles and nearly 100 switchbacks back down past Howard Lake to High Bridge, then the shuttle road (or shuttle bus, if timed right) back to Stehekin Landing. If early-season snow still covers the upper talus/glacier shelf, some parties glissade short, low-angle snow sections with an ice axe for self-arrest rather than downclimbing rock, but there is no fixed rappel infrastructure on this route.

This is a walk-off/scramble-down — no rappelling is documented (or generally needed) on Mount Dana or on the standard Dodwell-Rixon Pass access route. From the summit, reverse the ascent line: cross-country back west-southwest over the talus and heather benches to Dodwell-Rixon Pass, then down-climb the Elwha Snow Finger as the return route to Elwha Basin/Chicago Camp. Descending the Snow Finger is generally more hazard-prone than climbing it — a glissade is tempting on a mellow day but should be avoided if the moat at the base is open, if the surface has softened into slush, or if there's a risk of sliding into exposed rock (trip reports from this same drainage describe a nearby 'crevasse-like gap' where a stream undercuts the snow), so plan to face in and down-climb with an axe ready for self-arrest anywhere it steepens, particularly late season when the finger has thinned and pulled away from the surrounding rock walls. Below the snow, pick up the boot path back to Chicago Camp, re-ford the Elwha River, and rejoin the maintained Elwha River Trail for the long, gentle walk back down-valley (~24-26 miles) to Whiskey Bend — plus the current ~7-mile road walk/bike back to Madison Falls while the Olympic Hot Springs Road washout remains unrepaired. No technical anchors, fixed or natural, come into play anywhere on this route; the real crux of the descent is correctly reading the Snow Finger's snow condition and the scree/talus around the pass, not rope work.

This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, recross the Fairchild Glacier roped up with crampons, following the same wind-formed snow ridge back down to the ~6,700 ft access point, then regain Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill/traverse back across the Catwalk (or the north-side alternative) to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.

Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: down the North Ridge to the top of the chute, then down-climb the loose chute back to the valley floor — this is the most hazard-prone part of the descent, since the same scree and rockbands that were merely tedious going up become genuinely slippery and rockfall-prone with tired legs and no rope; move one at a time through any narrows and stay alert for parties below. At the bottom, re-ford the North Fork Quinault River (same knee-to-thigh-deep crossing as the approach — check levels, as afternoon snowmelt can raise it) to regain the maintained trail near Sixteen Mile camp, then simply walk the North Fork Quinault River Trail back out to the trailhead, re-fording Elip and Wild Rose Creeks en route. There is no rappelling on this route: it is a scramble/walk-off (Grade I, Class 3 via the North Ridge, 'Basic Snow/Rock Scramble', or Class 2 hiking), and nothing on it involves fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work — a hand line could be a reasonable precaution for a mixed-experience party on the loose upper chute or on lingering early-season snow, but it is not a technical necessity.

set.beta: Documented as an alternate class 3 scrambling line to Mount Lincoln's summit, climbing a chute/gully rather than the open south ridge; reached from the same Flapjack Lakes approach as the standard route. Detailed pitch-by-pitch or turn-by-turn beta is not available.

set.descent_text: The North Face is not descended — after topping out on the summit ridge (9,082 ft), descend via the standard South Slopes / south ridge walk-off: down the south ridge and upper talus to about 7,700 ft, then southwest down broad open slopes to the 6,840 ft saddle. From there most parties drop back into Leroy Creek Basin to retrieve camp and reverse the Leroy Creek climber's path and Phelps Creek Trail to the trailhead; some parties instead exit via the Ice Lakes basin and the Carne Mountain High Route depending on snow conditions and where camp/vehicles are staged, which several parties describe as an efficient alternative when the Maude/Seven Fingered Jack col has gone soft and mushy in the afternoon. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly reported on the standard descent line (the single technical rappel reported is on the approach traverse under the face, not the summit descent, and is conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route). Descent-specific hazards: loose 3rd-class rock and scree on the south ridge/upper slopes, a large cornice that forms on the summit ridge above the North Face's climber's-right side (stay well back from the edge near the top), lingering steep snow and possible rockfall in the col/gully area, and — if exiting toward Ice Lakes — extra route-finding and a longer, more remote tail to the car. Parties should budget real time for this descent; one party logged roughly 13 hours car-to-car including the North Face climb and this walk-off.

This is a walk-off/downclimb — reverse the ascent scramble route back over the Straight Creek Fault notch, chimney, and Knife's Edge ridge to Stujack Pass, then follow Trail #644 back down past Lake Metan to the trailhead. There is no rappelling on the standard route and no fixed rope stations. That said, the descent is not to be taken lightly: several trip reports flag the class 3 chimney/knife-edge section as harder to downclimb than to ascend because the exposure faces you directly, and multiple parties warn against blindly following cairns on the way down — stray cairns on Mount Pugh have been reported leading hikers toward vertical cliff bands requiring unplanned Class 4 downclimbing to regain the correct line. Downclimb the chimney facing in, use the iron ring as a handhold, and treat the permanent snowfield beside the ridge with care (an axe/careful step-kicking, or a short detour, if it's icy). Once back at Stujack Pass the descent is straightforward trail hiking, but the meadow and talus tread below the pass sloughs easily, so watch footing on the switchbacks. Plan to be off the exposed ridge before dark or bad weather moves in — the rock there is unpleasant and disorienting to navigate wet or in low light.

set.approach: The standard-route trailhead is the Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of Hwy 101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft elevation. Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels, not Mildred or Flapjack Lakes - those serve neighboring Mount Cruiser/Mount Lena out of the North Fork Skokomish/Staircase side. From the trailhead, Putvin Trail #812 is unmaintained for its last ~1.6 miles but well-traveled and easy to follow when snow-free; the tread is notably steep and narrow with unstable footing in spots as it climbs through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles in, the trail breaks into the open, grassy Whitehorse Creek basin and continues up to Lake of the Angels (about 3.5 miles and roughly 2,800-3,000 ft of gain from the trailhead, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace), a scenic alpine lake sitting in a cirque below Mount Stone and the Skokomish massif - this is the last reliable water source and the standard camp for an overnight trip. From the lake, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. From the saddle, a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn, before turning to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Total round-trip stats commonly cited are roughly 9-12 miles and about 5,000-5,100 ft of gain, with climbing parties reporting 3.5-5 hours up. Hazards: the narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread; lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes well into summer (reports note hazard even in August/September); and notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block, which is the crux of the route more than any single technical move.

set.rappel_count_note: 6 rappels total: 5 on the main line, plus an additional single rappel past the balanced-rock landmark before reaching easier ground.

set.descent_text: This is a glacier walk-up/scramble with no fixed rappel stations anywhere on the standard line — descent is a walk-off, reversing the ascent route. From the Sherman Peak/crater-rim high point, downclimb the steep snow of the upper Easton Glacier past the Roman Wall section first — most parties find this the psychologically hardest part of the day simply because of sustained steepness (roughly 30 degrees) right off the summit plateau; face-in plunge-stepping or a careful glissade (only when runout and snow conditions are safe, and never near crevasses or the crater's exposed rock) is typical. Continue back down through the Sherman Crater rim area, staying alert for the same fumarole/loose-rock hazard noted on the approach, then re-rope for the descent back through the Easton Glacier's crevasse field, following your ascent wands/tracks rather than freelancing a new line, since crevasse bridges can fail or shift through the day. Below the glacier's toe, pick up the Railroad Grade moraine-crest trail back to Sandy/High Camp and down through Morovitz Meadows to the Park Butte Trailhead, re-fording Sulfur Creek near the end. In good visibility this is a straightforward reverse of the route; in Baker's characteristic cloud cap or whiteout conditions, GPS/wands become essential since the moraine crest and crater rim offer little natural handrail. There is no roped rappelling on this route in normal conditions.
